extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, in-house counsel, and scholars analyzing patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing an issued patent's expected enforcement outcome using industry-specific empirical win-rates and claim-level quality markers (breadth, enablement, eligibility, prosecution history, and evidentiary fit to accused products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry baseline win rate
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the technology area's baseline win rate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical industry-level statistics to set expectations: overall patentees lose ~75% of merits decisions; trial patentees win ~60% (selection effect); chemical/pharma patents found valid and infringed >50% of the time, biotechnology ~5.6% win-rate, software ~14% (~1 in 7) for merits-decided cases. Apply the appropriate baseline when predicting an individual patent's expected outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival past summary judgment / pretrial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial outcomes differ from pretrial outcomes because weak patents are eliminated at summary judgment or earlier motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize selection: patents that proceed to trial are a positively selected subset. A patent's ability to survive motions to dismiss and summary judgment materially affects observed win rates; survival is a key quality signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous survival of validity and infringement findings
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent's enforcement success requires both validity and infringement findings to survive; quality requires the simultaneous survival of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate validity in isolation. A patent can be valid but not infringed (claims too narrow) or infringed but invalid (claims too broad). Best-quality patents survive both validity and infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goldilocks scope (breadth-narrowness tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad enough to read on competitor products, narrow enough to escape prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful claim drafting should place asserted claims in this narrow band. Overly broad claims invite invalidity; overly narrow claims risk noninfringement. Assess where asserted claims sit on this tradeoff as a core quality metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple asserted claim layers
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees typically assert several claims at varying breadth; quality patents have a defensible mid-tier claim that can survive validity while still reading on the accused product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and assert layered claims (broad, mid, narrow) so that if broad claims are invalidated, a defensible middle-ground claim remains to capture the accused product. Presence and defensibility of mid-tier claims is a positive quality indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear construction anchors (reduce Markman risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms with unambiguous construction (defined in spec, prosecution-history-supported, or settled in art) reduce Markman risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit definitions in the specification, consistent prosecution history, and citations to settled technical meaning where possible. Clear anchors reduce the chance of adverse claim construction and unpredictable scope shifts at Markman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution-history cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: A clean prosecution history (no estoppels, consistent claim interpretation) improves expected enforcement outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate file-wrapper for disclaimers, amendments, or arguments that could estop claim scope. Inconsistent statements or narrowing amendments increase invalidity/infringement risk and reduce expected enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility-safe drafting (Alice/Mayo/Bilski risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must avoid the 'abstract idea / natural phenomenon plus conventional steps' pattern; survival of Alice/Mayo motions is a key quality threshold, especially in software, biotech, and diagnostics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims emphasizing technical improvements, concrete implementations, or structural limitations rather than functional results. For life sciences, ensure claims do not recite mere natural phenomena without inventive application; for software, tie claims to technical solutions or hardware improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and written-description sufficiency (biotech/genus risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotech genus claims often fail enablement; quality biotech patents must show enablement of the full genus and a written description demonstrating possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support genus claims with representative examples, adequate experimental data, and disclosure of embodiments across the claimed scope. Ensure the specification shows possession of claimed inventions to survive enablement and written-description challenges (cf. Amgen v. Sanofi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural specificity for chemical/pharmaceutical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound claims with structural specificity and scope tied to formulation or compound correlate with higher enforcement success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft chemical/pharmaceutical claims to precise structural features and link claim scope to specific formulations or compounds. Robust ANDA defenses and surviving claim construction with a favorable (even broad) construction at Markman predict higher trial success in these industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-specific claim markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Software patents perform poorly unless claims recite specific technical implementation or are tied to particular hardware/improvements rather than generic computer-implemented results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor claims that describe how the software achieves a technical improvement, tie to particular hardware or architectural features, or otherwise avoid being framed as abstract ideas. Survival of Alice/Mayo dismissal motions is the critical early threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-essential / SEP status advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard-essential patents (SEPs) tend to perform better in enforcement than non-essential patents in computer hardware/semiconductor areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEP designation and related standards-context can increase the likelihood of enforcement success; evaluate whether the patent claims read on relevant standards and whether SEP-related remedies or licensing contexts apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence that accused product literally falls within claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there evidence the accused product clearly falls within the literal claim language?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual and technical records showing literal infringement (claim elements present in the accused product). Strong, documentable evidence of literal infringement materially raises the chance of enforcement success, particularly when paired with defensible claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection effects and representativeness caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents selected for litigation are systematically the strongest or most aggressively asserted, so litigated-patent statistics overstate average patent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using litigated-case statistics to infer general patent quality, adjust for selection bias: the 25% patentee-win rate among litigated patents implies lower expected validity in the unlitigated population. Industry comparisons may also reflect differing selection propensities.
